claim: Commonly used binary classification accuracy metrics, including the Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), are not actually independent of class prevalence and reference-standard quality as often assumed, causing their apparent values to deviate substantially from true classification accuracy.
method: The authors use simulated binary classification data with realistic parameters (e.g., from remote sensing applications) to compute multiple accuracy metrics (Recall, Precision, Specificity, NPV, J, F1, likelihood ratios, MCC) across varying levels of class prevalence and varying degrees of reference standard imperfection.
result: All examined metrics, including MCC, varied substantially with prevalence and reference standard quality, with MCC sometimes being greatly over- or under-estimated and even showing a high apparent value for a classifier performing no better than random chance.

verdict:
The claim shows substantial overlap with retrieved source [1], "Challenges in the real world use of classification accuracy metrics: From recall and precision to the Matthews correlation coefficient" (2023). The abstract of [1] explicitly states that "the apparent accuracy assessed can differ greatly from the true accuracy" and that "mis-estimation of classification accuracy metrics and associated mis-interpretations are often due to variations in prevalence and the use of an imperfect reference standard" — this is essentially the same core claim being evaluated, including the specific focus on MCC named in the title. This appears to be either the same paper or a very closely related prior publication by what looks like the same research group.

Source [2], "Ground Truth in Classification Accuracy Assessment: Myth and Reality" (2024), reinforces this overlap, as it uses simulations of realistic scenarios to explore how ground reference quality and class abundance affect apparent classification accuracy — matching the claim's method (simulated data, varying prevalence and reference standard quality) almost exactly, though it does not explicitly mention MCC in the abstract excerpt.

Given these two sources, the claim does not appear novel; it closely replicates or extends work already published by (apparently) the same authors or research program, particularly [1], which already covers MCC, prevalence, and reference standard quality together. The remaining sources ([3]–[8]) are unrelated to this specific methodological claim about metric independence assumptions. Overall, this claim substantially overlaps with [1] and [2], and should not be treated as a novel contribution without clarifying how it differs from this closely related prior work.
